questions.stem: A client with bipolar disorder who takes lithium carbonate 600 mg twice daily started hydrochlorothiazide for blood pressure 2 weeks ago. The client now has vomiting, diarrhea, coarse hand tremors, slurred speech and an unsteady gait. The lithium level drawn 12 hours after the last dose is 2.4 mEq/L (therapeutic 0.6 to 1.2 mEq/L), and the serum sodium is 131 mEq/L. Complete the diagram by placing the condition the client is most likely experiencing, 2 actions the nurse should take, and 2 parameters the nurse should monitor.

actions.text: Hold the lithium and notify the provider
Start IV 0.9% sodium chloride as prescribed
Give the next lithium dose with food to reduce the stomach upset
Restrict fluids and sodium to treat the low blood pressure
Give a dose of the prescribed loperamide for the diarrhea

parameters.text: Level of consciousness and neurological signs
Weight compared with last month's weight
Mood and sleep pattern each day

rationale.correct: Lithium toxicity is worsened by dehydration, low sodium, thiazides, NSAIDs and ACE inhibitors. Hold lithium, give saline, and monitor levels and neurological status.

perOption.c1: A level of 2.4 mEq/L with GI upset, coarse tremor, slurred speech and ataxia is moderate to severe lithium toxicity; thiazides raise lithium levels.
perOption.c2: Mania does not cause coarse tremors, ataxia and a high lithium level.
perOption.c3: GI symptoms alone could be a virus, but the neurological signs and high level show toxicity.
perOption.c4: No serotonergic drug was added, and clonus and fever are absent.
perOption.a1: Stopping lithium is the first step; the provider may also stop the thiazide.
perOption.a2: Saline corrects dehydration and low sodium and helps the kidneys clear lithium.
perOption.a3: Any further lithium worsens the toxicity.
perOption.a4: Low sodium and fluid make the kidneys hold on to lithium.
perOption.a5: Treating the diarrhea alone does not address the toxicity.
perOption.p1: Repeat levels show whether lithium is falling or whether dialysis is needed.
perOption.p2: Worsening confusion, seizures or coma show severe toxicity.
perOption.p3: Weight change over a month does not guide acute treatment.
perOption.p4: Mood is followed long term but does not show response to toxicity treatment.
perOption.p5: TSH is checked during long-term therapy, not to guide acute toxicity care.

questions.stem: A client is on day 7 of a continuous heparin infusion after a femoral-popliteal bypass. The platelet count has fallen from 268,000/mm3 on admission to 96,000/mm3. The nurse notes a new cold, pale, painful left foot with a weak pulse, and the client says the right calf is swollen and tender. There is no bleeding. Complete the diagram by placing the condition the client is most likely experiencing, 2 actions the nurse should take, and 2 parameters the nurse should monitor.

condition.text: Expected effect of the heparin dose

actions.text: Stop all heparin, including flushes, and notify the provider
Prepare to start a non-heparin anticoagulant such as argatroban as prescribed
Switch to enoxaparin injections in place of the heparin infusion
Give a platelet transfusion to raise the count
Start warfarin today at the usual dose to replace the heparin

parameters.text: Circulation, color and pulses in the legs

rationale.correct: Suspect HIT when platelets fall by half or more 5 to 10 days into heparin, especially with new clots. Stop all heparin, start a non-heparin anticoagulant and monitor platelets and circulation.

perOption.c1: A fall in platelets of more than 50% 5 to 10 days after starting heparin, with new clots, is heparin-induced thrombocytopenia.
perOption.c2: DIC causes bleeding and clotting with abnormal clotting times, usually with sepsis or trauma.
perOption.c3: ITP causes low platelets with bleeding, not new clots.
perOption.c4: Heparin does not normally lower platelets; this pattern is a dangerous immune reaction.
perOption.a1: All heparin exposure must stop, because it drives the reaction.
perOption.a2: Clients with HIT still need anticoagulation to prevent more clots.
perOption.a3: Low-molecular-weight heparin cross-reacts and must not be used in HIT.
perOption.a4: Platelet transfusions can worsen clotting in HIT and are avoided unless bleeding.
perOption.a5: Starting warfarin before the platelets recover can cause skin necrosis and limb gangrene.
perOption.p1: Recovery of the platelet count shows the reaction is resolving.
perOption.p2: Changes show whether the arterial and venous clots are improving or spreading.
perOption.p3: Glucose does not relate to HIT.
perOption.p4: Potassium is not a guide to HIT.
perOption.p5: Peak flow is used for asthma, not HIT.

questions.stem: A client is prescribed 1,000 mL of lactated Ringer's solution to infuse over 8 hours. No infusion pump is available on the unit after a power failure, so the nurse will regulate the infusion by gravity using tubing with a drop factor of 15 gtt/mL. How many drops per minute should the nurse set? Round to the nearest whole number.

rationale.correct: 1,000 mL / 480 minutes = 2.083 mL/min. 2.083 x 15 gtt/mL = 31.25, which rounds to 31 gtt/min.

questions.stem: A 4-year-old child who weighs 18 kg has acute otitis media with a fever of 38.9 °C (102 °F) and ear pulling for 2 days. The provider prescribes high-dose amoxicillin 90 mg/kg/day by mouth, divided into two doses every 12 hours. The pharmacy supplies amoxicillin oral suspension 400 mg/5 mL. How many milliliters should the nurse give for each dose? Round to one decimal place.

rationale.correct: Daily dose: 90 mg x 18 kg = 1,620 mg. Each dose: 1,620 / 2 = 810 mg. Volume: 810 mg / 400 mg x 5 mL = 10.125 mL, which rounds to 10.1 mL.

questions.stem: A client with treatment-resistant schizophrenia has taken clozapine for 3 months. The client now reports a sore throat and has a temperature of 38.6 °C (101.5 °F). What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Give acetaminophen and encourage fluids, then recheck the temperature in 4 hours
Hold the clozapine and notify the provider so an absolute neutrophil count can be checked
Ask the client whether anyone at home has had a cold or the flu in the past week
Give the clozapine as scheduled, since stopping it suddenly can cause the psychosis to return

rationale.correct: Clozapine can cause severe neutropenia. Fever, sore throat or other signs of infection mean holding the drug and checking the ANC right away.

perOption.a: Treating the fever alone may hide a life-threatening infection caused by low white cells.
perOption.b: Fever and sore throat in a client on clozapine may signal severe neutropenia (agranulocytosis); the drug is held until the ANC is known.
perOption.c: Exposure history is useful but does not address the immediate risk of agranulocytosis.
perOption.d: Relapse is a concern, but agranulocytosis is life-threatening and comes first.

questions.stem: A client who started lisinopril 10 days ago comes to the emergency department with swelling of the lips and tongue and a hoarse voice. The client has no hives or itching. Respirations are 22/min and SpO2 is 95% on room air. What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Give the client oral diphenhydramine and observe for 1 hour
Prepare for airway management and stay with the client while the provider is called
Tell the client to take the next lisinopril dose with a full glass of water and rest
Apply ice packs to the lips and tongue and recheck the amount of swelling in 30 minutes

rationale.correct: ACE inhibitor angioedema can happen at any time and can block the airway; protect the airway, stop the drug permanently and expect treatments other than antihistamines.

perOption.a: ACE inhibitor angioedema is caused by bradykinin, not histamine, so antihistamines work poorly; the airway comes first.
perOption.b: Tongue swelling and hoarseness signal possible airway obstruction; the nurse prepares for intubation and monitors closely.
perOption.c: The ACE inhibitor must be stopped permanently.
perOption.d: Cold packs do not treat airway swelling, and waiting is unsafe.

questions.stem: The nurse is reviewing teaching with a client who was prescribed levothyroxine for hypothyroidism. Which statement shows that the client understands how to take the drug?

options.text: "I'll take it with my calcium supplement and breakfast so I don't forget it."
"I'll take it on an empty stomach, 30 to 60 minutes before breakfast."
"I can stop taking it once my energy is back and I'm feeling like myself."
"I'll skip a dose whenever my heart feels like it's racing, then restart later."

rationale.correct: Take levothyroxine on an empty stomach at the same time each day, apart from calcium and iron, and continue it long term; report palpitations or chest pain.

perOption.a: Calcium, iron and food reduce levothyroxine absorption.
perOption.b: Levothyroxine is absorbed best on an empty stomach, taken at the same time each day.
perOption.c: Treatment for hypothyroidism is usually lifelong.
perOption.d: Palpitations may mean the dose is too high and should be reported, not managed by skipping doses.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information

questions.stem: A client is starting phenelzine, a monoamine oxidase inhibitor (MAOI), for depression. Which foods should the nurse teach the client to avoid? Select all that apply.

options.text: Aged cheddar cheese
Draft beer on tap
Fresh chicken breast cooked the same day
Soy sauce
Cured salami
Fresh apples

rationale.correct: With MAOIs, avoid tyramine-rich foods: aged cheeses, cured meats, tap beer, fermented soy and overripe or fermented foods.

perOption.a: Aged cheeses are high in tyramine, which can cause a hypertensive crisis with MAOIs.
perOption.b: Tap beer is high in tyramine.
perOption.c: Fresh meats are low in tyramine.
perOption.d: Fermented soy products are high in tyramine.
perOption.e: Cured and fermented meats are high in tyramine.

questions.stem: A client with type 1 diabetes who takes insulin glargine 24 units every evening is NPO after midnight for a colonoscopy tomorrow. What should the nurse expect for tonight's glargine dose?

options.text: Hold the glargine tonight because the client will not eat until after the procedure
Give a reduced dose of glargine tonight, as the provider prescribes, and check glucose
Give the glargine with a dose of rapid-acting insulin to cover tomorrow's fasting
Change the glargine to a sliding scale of regular insulin given at 2-hour intervals overnight

rationale.correct: In type 1 diabetes, basal insulin is never simply stopped; during fasting it is usually reduced and glucose is checked often.

perOption.a: Clients with type 1 diabetes need basal insulin at all times or they risk ketoacidosis.
perOption.b: Basal insulin is usually continued at a reduced dose (often about 75 to 80%) during fasting to prevent both hypoglycemia and ketoacidosis.
perOption.c: Rapid-acting insulin covers meals; giving it while fasting would cause hypoglycemia.
perOption.d: Sliding scale alone does not replace basal insulin in type 1 diabetes.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information

questions.stem: A 78-year-old client with heart failure is receiving a second unit of packed red blood cells. Ninety minutes into the unit, the client becomes short of breath with crackles in both lungs, blood pressure 178/96 mm Hg (it was 132/78), heart rate 108/min and distended neck veins. Temperature is unchanged. What should the nurse suspect?

options.text: An acute hemolytic reaction from ABO-incompatible blood
Transfusion-associated circulatory overload
A febrile non-hemolytic reaction to white cells in the unit
Transfusion-related acute lung injury from donor antibodies

rationale.correct: Transfusion-associated circulatory overload causes dyspnea, crackles, hypertension and distended neck veins; stop the transfusion, sit the client up, notify the provider and expect a diuretic.

perOption.a: Hemolytic reactions usually start within the first 15 minutes with fever, back pain and hypotension.
perOption.b: Dyspnea, crackles, hypertension and distended neck veins in an older client with heart failure suggest fluid overload from the transfusion.
perOption.c: Febrile reactions cause fever and chills, which are absent.
perOption.d: TRALI causes respiratory distress usually with hypotension and fever, not hypertension and distended neck veins.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Written to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026.

questions.stem: The nurse is preparing to give enoxaparin 40 mg subcutaneously from a prefilled syringe. Which technique is correct?

options.text: Expel the air bubble from the syringe before injecting the dose
Inject into the abdomen at least 5 cm (2 in) from the navel without rubbing afterward
Aspirate for blood before injecting to make sure that a blood vessel was not entered by the needle
Massage the site firmly for 1 minute after the injection to help absorption

rationale.correct: Enoxaparin: abdomen at least 5 cm from the navel, leave the air bubble, do not aspirate or rub, and rotate sites.

perOption.a: The air bubble in the prefilled syringe is left in so the full dose is given.
perOption.b: The abdomen away from the navel is the preferred site, and not rubbing reduces bruising.
perOption.c: Aspirating increases tissue damage and bruising with anticoagulants.

questions.stem: The nurse is preparing discharge teaching for four clients. For each medication, choose the most important instruction.

options.text: Stay upright for 30 minutes after taking it with a full glass of water
Take it with milk to protect the stomach
Take it at bedtime so it works overnight
Take it with grapefruit juice
Avoid all alcohol during therapy and for 3 days after
Expect urine to turn bright orange
Avoid salt substitutes that contain potassium
Eat a banana every day to replace potassium
Take it at bedtime to avoid daytime urination
Take it with a glass of milk
Take it with antacids to prevent upset
Take it on an empty stomach and use sunscreen outdoors

rationale.correct: Teach the instruction that prevents the most serious problem: esophagitis with alendronate, alcohol reactions with metronidazole, hyperkalemia with spironolactone, poor absorption and sunburn with tetracycline.

perOption.b1:a: Staying upright prevents esophageal irritation and ulcers.
perOption.b1:c: Lying down after the dose risks esophagitis.
perOption.b2:a: Grapefruit is not the concern with metronidazole.
perOption.b2:b: Alcohol with metronidazole causes a disulfiram-like reaction.
perOption.b3:a: Spironolactone keeps potassium in the body; potassium salt substitutes can cause hyperkalemia.
perOption.b3:b: Extra potassium is risky with a potassium-sparing diuretic.
perOption.b3:c: Diuretics are usually taken in the morning.
perOption.b4:a: Dairy binds tetracycline and blocks absorption.
perOption.b4:c: Food and dairy reduce absorption, and tetracycline causes photosensitivity.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
Written to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client with rheumatoid arthritis is prescribed oral methotrexate 15 mg once a week. During a follow-up call, the client says, "I've been taking one dose every morning, like my blood pressure pill." The client reports mouth sores and bruising. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Tell the client to skip tomorrow's dose and then go back to taking one tablet each morning as before
Tell the client to stop the methotrexate and arrange urgent assessment by the provider today
Suggest a saltwater rinse for the mouth sores and continue the current schedule
Ask the client to bring the pill bottle to the next routine appointment next month

rationale.correct: Low-dose methotrexate is taken once a week; accidental daily dosing causes life-threatening toxicity and needs urgent assessment.

perOption.a: Daily dosing is a dangerous error; continuing it could be fatal.
perOption.b: Daily methotrexate causes toxicity such as mucositis and bone marrow suppression; the client needs urgent labs and possibly leucovorin.
perOption.c: This treats a symptom and ignores the overdose.
perOption.d: Waiting a month risks severe bone marrow suppression.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
Written to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client had an ileostomy created 4 days ago. The ostomy has put out 1,900 mL of liquid stool in the last 24 hours. The client is dizzy when standing, the mouth is dry and urine is dark amber. What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Empty the pouch more often and check that it seals well around the stoma
Report the high output and signs of dehydration to the provider
Encourage the client to drink plain water freely to replace the fluid lost
Teach the client to eat more fresh fruit and raw vegetables to thicken the stool

rationale.correct: High ileostomy output (more than about 1.5 L/day) can quickly cause dehydration and low sodium and potassium; report it and expect fluid and electrolyte replacement.

perOption.a: Pouch care matters, but it does not address the fluid loss.
perOption.b: High ileostomy output with dizziness and concentrated urine signals dehydration and electrolyte loss that needs treatment.
perOption.c: Large amounts of plain water can increase output and lower sodium; oral rehydration solutions are preferred.
perOption.d: High-fiber raw foods can increase output or block the stoma.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)

questions.educationalObjective: Recognize dehydration from high ileostomy output.

questions.stem: The nurse is reviewing requests for a heating pad from four clients. For which client is applying heat contraindicated?

options.text: A client with chronic low back muscle spasm who has had back pain for 2 years and uses a heating pad at home
A client with right lower quadrant pain, fever and rebound tenderness that is not yet diagnosed
A client with osteoarthritis of the knee who reports stiffness each morning
A client with menstrual cramps who has no other abdominal symptoms or fever

rationale.correct: Avoid heat over undiagnosed abdominal pain, active bleeding, acute injuries in the first 24 to 48 hours, areas of poor sensation and malignancies.

perOption.a: Heat relaxes chronic muscle spasm and is appropriate.
perOption.b: Heat to the abdomen of a client with possible appendicitis can speed rupture; heat is avoided over undiagnosed abdominal pain.
perOption.c: Heat eases joint stiffness in osteoarthritis.
perOption.d: Heat is a common comfort measure for menstrual cramps.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)

questions.stem: A client with left-sided weakness after a stroke is learning to walk with a single-point cane. Which observation shows the client is using the cane correctly?

options.text: The client holds the cane in the left hand and moves it with the left leg
The client holds the cane in the right hand and moves it forward with the left leg
The client holds the cane in the right hand and moves it forward with the right leg
The client holds the cane in front of the body with both hands for balance

rationale.correct: Hold the cane on the strong side and move it forward with the weak leg.

perOption.a: The cane is held on the strong side, not the weak side.
perOption.b: Holding the cane on the strong side and moving it with the weak leg widens the base of support.
perOption.c: The cane should move with the weak leg so the two share the weight.
perOption.d: A single-point cane is used on one side, not with both hands.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)

questions.stem: A client with a neurogenic bladder after a spinal cord injury is learning clean intermittent self-catheterization for use at home. Which statement shows the client needs more teaching?

options.text: "I'll wash my hands with soap and water before I catheterize."
"I'll catheterize on a regular schedule, about 4 to 6 hours apart."
"I'll wait until I feel my bladder is full before I catheterize."
"I'll call if my urine becomes cloudy or smells bad, or I get a fever."

rationale.correct: Intermittent self-catheterization uses clean technique on a set schedule, because sensation of fullness may be absent.

perOption.a: Hand hygiene is part of clean technique.
perOption.b: A regular schedule prevents overdistention and infection.
perOption.c: After spinal cord injury the client may not feel fullness; waiting risks overdistention and autonomic dysreflexia.
perOption.d: These are signs of urinary tract infection to report.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)

questions.stem: A client receives continuous enteral feeding through a nasogastric tube at 60 mL/hr. Review the nurse's note and highlight the findings that suggest the client is not tolerating the feeding.

segments.text: The client reports nausea and has vomited once
Bowel sounds present in four quadrants
Tube marking unchanged at 55 cm at the nostril

rationale.correct: Feeding intolerance: distention, nausea, vomiting and diarrhea. Pause or slow the feeding per policy and notify the provider.

perOption.s2: Distention suggests the stomach is not emptying.
perOption.s4: Nausea and vomiting are signs of intolerance and raise aspiration risk.
perOption.s8: Stable external length suggests the tube has not moved.
perOption.s10: Diarrhea can signal intolerance, a fast rate or another cause such as infection.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)

questions.stem: A client with stage 4 chronic kidney disease who is not on dialysis has a potassium of 5.6 mEq/L and a phosphorus of 5.9 mg/dL. The client asks the nurse for a snack. Which choice is best?

options.text: A ripe banana with a glass of low-fat milk
Apple slices with a few unsalted crackers
A cup of yogurt topped with almonds
A baked potato with cheese and a cola

rationale.correct: In CKD with high potassium and phosphorus, choose low-potassium fruits such as apples and berries and avoid dairy, nuts, colas, potatoes and bananas.

perOption.a: Bananas are high in potassium and milk is high in potassium and phosphorus.
perOption.b: Apples and unsalted crackers are low in potassium, phosphorus and sodium.
perOption.c: Dairy and nuts are high in phosphorus and potassium.
perOption.d: Potatoes are high in potassium; cheese and cola are high in phosphorus.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)

questions.stem: A client had a total hip replacement through a posterior approach yesterday. Which action by an assistive personnel (AP) requires the nurse to intervene?

options.text: Placing an abduction pillow between the client's legs while they lie in bed
Helping the client sit in a high chair with firm arms for breakfast
Letting the client cross their legs at the ankles while resting in bed
Using a raised toilet seat when the client walks to the bathroom

rationale.correct: After a posterior hip replacement: no crossing legs, no hip flexion past 90 degrees and no internal rotation; use abduction pillows and raised seats.

perOption.a: The pillow keeps the legs apart and helps prevent dislocation.
perOption.b: A high chair keeps hip flexion below 90 degrees.
perOption.c: Crossing the legs moves the hip toward adduction and can dislocate a posterior hip replacement.
perOption.d: A raised seat limits hip flexion.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)

questions.stem: A client in hospice care is in the last days of life. Which comfort measures should the nurse include? Select all that apply.

options.text: Moisten the mouth and lips with swabs and a lip balm
Insist the client eat three meals a day to keep up their strength
Give prescribed opioids for pain or breathlessness on a regular schedule
Turn and reposition the client gently for comfort
Encourage the family to talk to and touch the client
Wake the client every 2 hours to check orientation

rationale.correct: End-of-life comfort: mouth care, symptom relief with opioids, gentle repositioning, family presence and no forced intake.

perOption.a: Mouth breathing dries the mouth; moisture relieves discomfort.
perOption.b: Appetite falls near death; forcing food can cause distress and aspiration.
perOption.c: Opioids relieve both pain and dyspnea at the end of life.
perOption.d: Gentle turning prevents pressure and stiffness.
perOption.e: Hearing may remain to the end, and presence comforts both client and family.
perOption.f: Frequent waking disturbs rest and has no benefit at this stage.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Written to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Provide comfort care at the end of life.

questions.stem: A child has a new long-arm fiberglass cast after a forearm fracture. The parent says the child keeps complaining that the skin under the cast itches. What should the nurse teach the parent?

options.text: Slide a smooth ruler or a knitting needle under the cast to scratch the itch
Blow cool air from a hair dryer on the cool setting into the edge of the cast
Pour a little baby powder or lotion inside the cast to soothe the skin
Wrap the cast in a plastic bag and soak it in a cool bath for 10 minutes to soothe the skin

rationale.correct: Relieve cast itching with cool air; never put objects, powders or lotions under a cast, and keep it dry.

perOption.a: Objects under the cast can break the skin and cause infection or pressure injury.
perOption.b: Cool air relieves itching without injuring the skin.
perOption.c: Powders and lotions clump under the cast and irritate the skin.
perOption.d: Soaking can damage the padding and macerate the skin.

questions.stem: A hospitalized client says they cannot sleep because staff come in every hour during the night. Which action is most likely to improve the client's sleep?

options.text: Group night-time care, such as vital signs and medications, into as few visits as possible
Ask the provider for a prescription for a sleeping pill that the client can take each night
Leave the overhead light on so staff do not need to turn it on and wake the client
Move the client to a room closer to the nurses' station so that the night checks are quicker

rationale.correct: Cluster care at night, reduce noise and light and keep a regular routine to support sleep in the hospital.

perOption.a: Clustering care allows longer periods of uninterrupted sleep.
perOption.b: Medication should not be the first choice; it does not reduce interruptions.
perOption.d: Rooms near the station are often noisier.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)

questions.stem: A client with borderline personality disorder tells the night nurse, "You're the only one here who understands me. The day nurses are cruel and won't let me use my phone after 9." The unit rule is that phones are collected at 2100. What is the nurse's best response?

options.text: "I'll let you keep your phone tonight, since you've had a hard day with the day staff."
"The phone rule is the same with each nurse on the unit. Let's talk about how you're feeling tonight."
"I'll speak to the day nurses tomorrow about how they've been treating you on this unit."
"You're manipulating the staff, and that behavior is not acceptable on this unit."

rationale.correct: Respond to splitting with consistent limits from the whole team, without taking sides, while acknowledging the client's feelings.

perOption.a: Bending rules for one client rewards splitting and undermines the team.
perOption.b: Consistent limits across staff counter splitting, and inviting talk about feelings supports the client.
perOption.c: Taking sides supports splitting staff into good and bad.
perOption.d: Labeling the behavior is confrontational and harms the therapeutic relationship.

references: Psychiatric-mental health nursing texts (e.g. Varcarolis; Halter)

questions.educationalObjective: Respond to splitting in borderline personality disorder.

questions.stem: A 5-year-old child whose grandparent died last week asks the nurse, "When will Grandpa come back from being dead?" How should the nurse understand this question?

options.text: The child is in denial and needs referral to a grief counselor
The child sees death as temporary or reversible, which is typical at this age
The child has not been told about the death and needs to be told today
The child is confused because of the stress of the whole family's grief over the past week

rationale.correct: Preschoolers see death as temporary; by about 9 or 10, children understand it is permanent and universal. Use simple, honest words such as "died."

perOption.a: This is a typical developmental understanding, not denial needing referral.
perOption.b: Preschoolers often think death is reversible; simple, honest explanations help.
perOption.c: The question shows the child knows about the death but not its permanence.
perOption.d: Stress may add to confusion, but the main reason is the child's stage of thinking.

references: Pediatric nursing texts (e.g. Hockenberry, Wong's Essentials of Pediatric Nursing)
Psychiatric-mental health nursing texts (e.g. Varcarolis; Halter)
